title: Apes Have Inner Circles Too
hook: Chimps and bonobos build friendships much like we do — a tight inner circle of close partners surrounded by a wider ring of looser ties.
key_points: Researchers studied grooming to map how chimpanzees and bonobos bond.
Both apes form a small inner circle of close friends plus weaker outer connections.
Chimpanzees focus on a few trusted partners and grow more selective with age.
Bonobos keep a more egalitarian, evenly spread social style.
content_html: Friendship may not be a uniquely human thing. By tracking grooming — who grooms whom, and how often — researchers found that chimpanzees and bonobos build social lives that look a lot like ours, reported by ScienceDaily. Each ape keeps a small inner circle of close, trusted partners, wrapped in a wider network of weaker, more casual connections.
extra_html: The two species play it differently, though. Chimpanzees tend to concentrate on a few trusted friends and become more selective as they age, narrowing their circle over time. Bonobos, by contrast, keep a more egalitarian style, spreading their bonds more evenly across the group rather than playing favorites. The familiar structure — a tight core plus looser acquaintances — echoes how human social circles are often described, which is why the researchers call these friendship patterns "human-like."
